html:
ISO 42001 AI governance is becoming increasingly important as AI systems move from simply processing data to making inferences that can shape decisions, opportunities and interventions.

We have spent two decades building a fortress around the extraction machine. Encryption. Consent mechanisms. Retention schedules. Breach notification. Much of this has focused on securing the collection, storage and processing of personal data.

Far less attention has gone to a simpler question: what is being inferred about people; and what happens because of it?

This is the shift Shoshana Zuboff’s work on surveillance capitalism brought into focus. Behavioural surplus becomes prediction products. Prediction products become behavioural futures markets. And AI is industrialising the middle step. In the age of inference, prediction is no longer a by-product of a service. In some systems, it is the service.

The concern is not only that data is collected. Decisions, opportunities and interventions are increasingly shaped by statistical inferences about people, often without those affected having meaningful visibility into how the inferences are produced, used or challenged.

This is where ISO/IEC 42001 becomes relevant: it provides a governance framework for examining how AI systems create, use and act on inferences about people.

It does not ban profiling. It does not outlaw automated decision-making. And it does not, by itself, eliminate surveillance capitalism.

What it provides is a management-system framework through which the risks and impacts associated with AI systems can be identified, assessed and governed.

Three areas stand out.

1. AI policy and accountability

    Clause 5 establishes the organisational foundation for responsible AI by requiring policy, leadership, defined responsibilities and integration of the AI management system into organisational processes. These mechanisms make accountability for AI-enabled inferences an operational responsibility rather than an abstract principle.

    2. AI risk and impact assessment

    This is where ISO/IEC 42001 becomes particularly interesting from an autonomy perspective.

    Clause 6 requires organisations to establish processes for AI risk assessment and treatment.

    More importantly, Clause 6.1.4 requires an AI system impact assessment that considers potential consequences for individuals, groups and societies arising from the development, provision or use of AI systems, including their intended use and foreseeable misuse.

    Annex A.5 reinforces this by addressing the assessment of AI system impacts throughout the AI system life cycle.

    That creates a governance mechanism for asking a question that conventional technology risk assessments can easily overlook:

    What happens to the people affected by the system?

    Profiling, behavioral prediction, inappropriate automation and other forms of AI-enabled influence can therefore be considered as potential impacts and risks, depending on the organisation’s context and assessment.

    3. Responsible use and human oversight

    ISO/IEC 42001 does not simply ask whether an AI system works.

    Annex A.9 addresses the responsible use of AI systems. Its implementation guidance identifies objectives such as fairness, accountability, transparency, explainability, reliability, safety, privacy and security.

    The guidance also addresses meaningful human oversight. Depending on the intended use, this may involve reviewers checking AI outputs, authorised personnel overriding AI decisions where appropriate, ongoing performance monitoring, mechanisms for reporting concerns, and an explicit assessment of whether automated decision-making is suitable.

    That is important because the question is not simply:

    “Can the AI make this decision?”

    It is also:

    “Should the AI be making this decision without meaningful human involvement?”

    Surveillance-Capitalist Inference vs. 42001-Aligned Governance

    The point is not that ISO/IEC 42001 bans inference.

    It doesn’t.

    The point is that ISO/IEC 42001 creates a structure in which the consequences of AI systems become part of organisational governance through policy, risk assessment, impact assessment, responsible-use objectives, controls, documentation and accountability.

    That changes the question.

    Instead of asking only:

    “Was the data collected lawfully?”

    we increasingly need to ask:

    “What did the system infer, what did it do with that inference, who was affected, and who was accountable for the outcome?”

    In the age of inference, autonomy should not simply be an unintended consequence of the model’s operation.

    It should be a governance consideration.

    Article by Ezekiel Makori
